segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, these versions of the verb that we get after haber, and we said that it's any version of haber,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ha, whether it's he, whether it's había, whether it's habría, we could even say "I will have".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I will have lost it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo habré perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Any version of haber, we will have the -ado/-ido version afterwards, even if it's in the "to" form.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We could say something like, "I would like to have gone". "I would like to have gone".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I would like, it would please me"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me gustaría...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...to have gone.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...haber ido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me gustaría haber ido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "It would please me to have gone. I would like to have gone".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me gustaría haber ido. So, even after the "to" form, we're having just one version of the verb that can come after haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now this version of the verb that can come after haber is very useful because if it makes sense,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: we can use it as an adjective, just as we can in English. For example,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: in English we say, "I have sold" and "sold" we can use like an adjective. We can say "it is sold".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We say, "I have lost" and we can use it like an adjective: "I am lost".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you can do the same in Spanish, which gives you hundreds and hundreds of words now that you can access as adjectives.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for example, "to close" is cerrar. Cerrar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cerrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, "I have closed it"? "I have closed it".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo he cerrado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo he cerrado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might be referring to the door, which is la puerta.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, if you were referring to the door, how would you say that: "I have closed it"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La he cerrado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La he cerrado. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, cerrado, we can take that and we can use it as an adjective.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, it doesn't change ever after haber. It's always cerrado. Lo he cerrado, la he cerrado, lo hemos cerrado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But when it's an adjective, when it's behaving like an adjective, then of course it can change. So, if you say, "it is closed",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and you mean the door, how will you say it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cerrada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, how would you say that: "it is closed"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es cerrada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Do you think "to be closed" is a state or a characteristic?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está cerrada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está cerrada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In fact, the great majority, with just a couple of exceptions, of these adjectives that we get from -ado/-ido, that we get from the version that comes after haber,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: go with estar. With this particular type of adjective, we don't need to really think about whether it's a state or a characteristic. They're just going to go with estar, with a couple of exceptions.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To lose" was...?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Perder.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is the version that comes after haber, after any form of haber? Perder becomes...?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Perdido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perdido. So, how would you say, "I am lost"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy perdido, or, female: perdida.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good! Estoy perdido, or for feminine: perdida. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "to finish" or "to terminate"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Terminar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Terminar. How would you say, "I have finished"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, now you can also say "it is finished" and use it like an adjective.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está terminado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Está terminado. What if you were referring to the movie, which is la película?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está terminada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Está terminada. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, this gives us a lot of adjectives we can access. Let's have a look at some of them. "To sell" was vender, and then "sold" would be...?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vendido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "They are sold"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Están vendidos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Están vendidos. And if we mean las casas, how will it sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Están vendidas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Están vendidas. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Some of the adjectives that we already met are actually adjectives that were formed in this way. How was the word for "tired"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cansado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cansado. And this comes from the verb cansar, "to tire".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Huh? So, cansar is "to tire" and then cansado is the version that you get after haber and it's the adjective: cansado, "tired".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, if you want to say, "I get tired, I tire myself", so now it's present...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me canso.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me canso. That means "I get tired" or even "I get fed up".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, "I have tired myself"? And like I said, it doesn't literally mean that you are responsible for tiring yourself. It just means you've got tired or you can use it like, "I've had enough".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I have tired myself"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He... me he cansado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me he cansado. "I have gotten tired, I've gotten fed up". Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then cansado, which is the version of cansar after haber is also of course the adjective, "tired".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I am tired"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy cansada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, "to close" is cerrar and we said that "closed" is cerrado,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and we said that these -ado/-ido adjectives, with a couple of exceptions, go with estar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, how do you say, "it is closed"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está cerrado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say, "he is closed to the idea"? "Idea" is the same word in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "He is closed to the idea".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está cerrado a el idea...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What gender does it look like, idea?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La idea.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está cerrado a la idea. "He's closed to the idea".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you want to say he's a closed person, you mean as a person he's closed, how do you think you would say it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es un person cerrado?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Almost. This is exactly the structure that we want, well done, but the word for "person" is feminine and it doesn't refer to anybody specifically, just the word itself is feminine.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es una persona cerrado... cerrada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cerrada refers to persona. Very good. Es una persona

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: cerrada. So, that's how we can get around that if we want to say he's closed and we mean he's a closed person. If we just say es cerrado,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: it sounds like a mistake, but es una persona cerrada is fine because es is going with persona. What you're saying essentially is "he is a person

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: that is closed". Es una persona cerrada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, "she is lost"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está perdida.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Está perdida, "she's lost". But if you want to say she's lost, you know, as a person, she's lost her way...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es una persona perdida.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well, actually, why not estar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In this structure, you're saying "she is a person". You're not looking at "lost person", you're looking at "person".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The adjective is totally secondary. So, when you say "this is a chair",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you're going to use ser. If you're going to say "it's a wet chair",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: even though that is a state, you're still going to use ser because what you're saying is "it's a chair". The adjective is secondary.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you say "it is wet", then you use estar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "chair" or "seat" is silla.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Silla.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Silla.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Mojar, mojar means "to wet".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mojar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, how do you think you say "wet" as an adjective?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mojada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, for silla: mojada, in feminine. Good. So, how would you say, "the chair"...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: la silla,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "the chair is wet"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La silla está mojada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La silla está mojada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you say, "it is a wet chair", you're just saying "it is a chair"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and then the adjective is secondary. And the fact that it is a chair is about as characteristic as it gets.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, you're saying, "it is a chair"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es una silla...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...wet.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...mojada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Es una silla mojada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, when we say something is a noun, when we give it its name, there's nothing more

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: characteristic. Es una persona, "it is a person".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "It is a happy person": es una persona feliz.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "It's a chair": es una silla. "It's a wet chair":

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: es una silla mojada. The structure there is "it is a chair". The adjective is secondary.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But when we say "the chair is wet", then we are talking about a state of the chair with is:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: la silla está mojada. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.
